what: Every claim of every article: kind, text, section anchor, the quote it rests on, what it is about, its value if a data point.

claims.text: A plan to make a custom Firefox with a Ruflo hive of Claude Code workers, an sgit vault as its memory and a behaviour policy as its mandate, for the laptop and the iPad.
claims.quote: a plan to make a custom Firefox with the workflow we showed at the agentics talk

claims.text: The workflow is a hive, a memory and a mandate: Ruflo gives the hands, an sgit vault the memory, and an Agent Behaviour Policy gives each role its mandate.
claims.quote: a hive, a memory and a mandate

claims.text: The plan is a proposal that the owner has not run yet, and it says so where it matters.
claims.quote: The plan below is a proposal: I have not run it yet

claims.text: The plan starts as explorer coding: the owner writes the wants in his own words, the list goes into the vault, and it is the brief.
claims.quote: That list goes into the vault, and it is the brief.

claims.text: For each want the first worker finds the lowest layer that delivers it, because every layer up is more to maintain.
claims.quote: for each want, find the lowest layer that delivers it, because every layer up is more to maintain

claims.text: Firefox reads a policies.json from a distribution folder; policies cover menus, home page, search, extensions and the AI sidebar, survive updates and need almost no maintenance.
claims.quote: They survive updates and need almost no maintenance.

claims.text: A userChrome.css in the profile can restyle or hide any part of the browser's interface; it is the most powerful layer without code and the least stable, because it is unsupported.
claims.quote: It is the most powerful layer without code, and the least stable

claims.text: Extensions need to be signed by Mozilla, an unlisted one is signed and then distributed by the owner, and extensions cannot restructure the browser.
claims.quote: They cannot restructure the browser.

claims.text: A personal fork is a small patch set on top of the release, the way LibreWolf carries 63 patches and Debian 17, applied to each new version.
claims.quote: carries 63 patches and Debian 17, applied to each new version

value.unit: patches LibreWolf carries on Firefox

claims.text: Firefox's artifact mode downloads pre-built C++ components, so a change to the interface does not need the full compile.
claims.quote: downloads pre-built C++ components rather than building them locally

claims.text: A full Firefox build is within reach on a laptop: Mozilla asks for 8 GB of memory and 30 GB of disk.
claims.quote: 8 GB of memory and 30 GB of disk

value.unit: GB of memory for a full build, with 30 GB of disk

claims.text: Mozilla's trademark policy forbids distributing a modified Firefox under that name, so a personal fork has to be renamed; only Mozilla can ship a custom build called Firefox.
claims.quote: you may not distribute a modified form of Firefox and continue to call it Firefox

claims.text: Apple's App Review Guideline 2.5.6 requires apps that browse the web to use WebKit, with exceptions only in the EU and Japan.
claims.quote: Apps that browse the web must use the appropriate WebKit framework

claims.text: Mozilla has decided not to build Gecko for iOS because a separate build would mean doubling the size of its iOS team.
claims.quote: would mean we would basically have to double the size of our iOS team

claims.text: Firefox for iOS is a separate Swift codebase on WebKit, none of the desktop layers exist there, and the only route is a fork built in Xcode and installed on the owner's iPad.
claims.quote: The only route is a fork of that codebase, changed by the hive, built in Xcode and installed on my own iPad.

claims.text: With a free Apple account the install lasts 7 days on up to 3 devices; a paid developer account gives a year and TestFlight.
claims.quote: the install lasts 7 days

value.unit: days an install lasts with a free Apple account

claims.text: The maintenance loop: each Firefox release starts a run in which the hive rebases the patches, rebuilds, tests each want, compares screenshots and reports, and the owner approves or refuses.
claims.quote: the hive rebases the patches, rebuilds, tests each want, compares screenshots and reports

claims.text: Since Firefox 155 on 1 September a new major release is made every two weeks, so a fork has 26 releases a year to follow, on each of two codebases.
claims.quote: so a fork has 26 releases a year to follow, on each of two codebases

value.unit: Firefox releases a year

claims.text: LibreWolf, with a team, ships within three days of each upstream release; Waterfox's maintainer describes a project often run by one person and a few months in the red.
claims.quote: a few months in the red recently

claims.text: The behaviour policy says what no worker may do: change anything but the front end, weaken security, updates or signing, use Mozilla's trademarks, or ship without the owner's approval.
claims.quote: change anything but the front end, weaken security, updates or signing, use Mozilla's trademarks, or ship without my approval

claims.text: PortGPT, a research system for porting Linux patches to older versions, reported an 89.15% success rate on 1,815 cases.
claims.quote: a research system for porting Linux patches to older versions, reported

value.unit: percent of patch-porting cases

claims.text: The owner found no browser fork maintained without people checking the result, so the plan has him read the report and approve every release.
claims.quote: I read the report and approve every release

claims.text: Mozilla should sell to one person what it sells to organisations: explore for free, keep it working for about 50p a release, a change built properly for £50 to £500.
claims.quote: I think it should sell the same to one person

claims.text: On 12 October Mozilla introduced Firefox Enterprise, with its own branding and a management console, and its paid support offers custom development options.
claims.quote: On 12 October it introduced

claims.text: Keeping a customisation tested against each release at about 50p a release comes to £13 a year.
claims.quote: That is £13 a year.

value.unit: GBP a year at about 50p a release

claims.text: Mozilla is better placed than the owner to keep a custom Firefox working: it alone can ship a modified build called Firefox, it signs extensions, it builds the next release and it maintains both codebases.
claims.quote: Mozilla is better placed than I am

claims.text: Mozilla depends on royalties for about three quarters of its revenue, and charging per version or per change is the income its chief executive meant by diversifying beyond search.
claims.quote: the kind of income its chief executive meant by

claims.text: The plan has not been run; every step is checked against the documentation, not tried end to end.
claims.quote: It is a plan; every step is checked against the documentation, not tried end to end.

claims.text: The prices are illustrative, the owner's and not Mozilla's.
claims.quote: The prices are illustrative. Mine, not Mozilla's.

claims.text: Mozilla's consumer offer does not exist; its enterprise build and support do, and their prices are not public.
claims.quote: Its enterprise build and support do; their prices are not public.

claims.text: No agent maintains a browser fork alone; the plan keeps a person approving every release.
claims.quote: No agent maintains a browser fork alone.

claims.text: The iPad route needs a developer account and only changes what Firefox for iOS can change on WebKit.
claims.quote: The iPad route needs a developer account.

claims.text: The article comes from a voice memo of the owner on 16 October 2026, written by the site's agent in the voice of the site.
claims.quote: A voice memo of mine on 16 October 2026

claims.text: Send a CISO to the newsroom as a CISO, a data protection officer as a DPO, and one particular person as a persona made for them, with nothing but a link.
claims.quote: This is the brief for doing that with nothing but a link.

claims.text: Personas move out of the site's code into an encrypted vault opened in the reader's browser with a published read key, so the newsroom's agents can add or update one without a change to the site.
claims.quote: Personas move out of the site's code into an encrypted vault

claims.text: There are three kinds of link: a page of its own for the few personas everyone uses, a fragment for any number more, and a private persona in its own vault.
claims.quote: A page of its own for the few personas everyone uses

claims.text: The site is static pages on GitHub Pages, so no server can answer an arbitrary persona path; the fragment after the hash solves it.
claims.quote: The site is static pages on GitHub Pages, so there is no server to answer

claims.text: RFC 3986 says the fragment is separated before dereference and dereferenced solely by the user agent, so the browser keeps it and GitHub Pages never sees it.
claims.quote: the browser keeps it, and GitHub Pages never sees it

claims.text: A private persona lives in a vault of its own and the link carries the vault id and read key: whoever has the link can open it, whoever does not cannot find out it exists.
claims.quote: Whoever has the link can open the persona; whoever does not, cannot, and cannot find out it exists.

claims.text: When the link opens, the page shows who you are reading as, the newsroom opens as that persona, and the persona is added to the reader's personas straight away as a visitor.
claims.quote: The persona is added to the reader's personas straight away, as a visitor

claims.text: Follow keeps the persona linked to the vault and Make it mine forks it; the two halves come straight from git, tracking the upstream or branching from it.
claims.quote: Follow and fork are the two halves of the design, and they come straight from git

claims.text: The site already opens thirty-odd vaults in the browser with nothing but an endpoint, a vault id and a read key, so a persona vault is one more.
claims.quote: This site already opens thirty-odd vaults that way

value.unit: vaults the site already opens in the browser

claims.text: The newsroom's agents keep the personas: every published article is added to the personas it belongs to, every newsletter is a review, and each change is a vault commit with a line in changes.jsonl.
claims.quote: Keeping personas is one more job on the desk.

claims.text: Adding or changing a persona is an sgit commit and push to the vault, without a release of the website, a build or a deploy.
claims.quote: without a release of the website, a build, or a deploy

claims.text: A persona can later carry outside reading with sources, which is how a newsroom with sixty articles can serve a dozen audiences well.
claims.quote: That is how a newsroom with sixty articles can serve a dozen audiences well

claims.text: Netflix launched Profiles on 1 August 2013, up to five per account, so each person in a household got their own suggestions.
claims.quote: Netflix launched Profiles on 1 August 2013, up to five per account

value.unit: profiles per Netflix account

claims.text: Bluesky's starter packs, launched 26 June 2024, each hold up to 150 people and three custom feeds and have their own link.
claims.quote: Each holds up to 150 people and three custom feeds, has its own link

value.unit: people per starter pack

claims.text: Starter packs are the closest thing to a link to a persona shipped at scale: the link is the onboarding, and what it sets up belongs to the newcomer afterwards.
claims.quote: the link is the onboarding, and what the link sets up belongs to the newcomer afterwards

claims.text: Mastodon's community follow packs were CSV files of up to 35 accounts, and the project has announced a native version whose people can opt out.
claims.quote: were CSV files of up to 35 accounts that a user downloaded and imported

value.unit: accounts per Mastodon follow pack

claims.text: A persona about a person goes in a private vault and is sent only to them; a public persona describes a role, never a named individual unless they have agreed.
claims.quote: a public persona describes a role, never a named individual, unless they have agreed

claims.text: Apple News and Brave News personalise on the device but still run servers; here the content is static files and the personas ciphertext, and the difference is who holds the copy that travels.
claims.quote: the difference is who holds the copy that travels between devices

claims.text: A persona here is not a fictional user a team designs for; it is a reading list the reader wears and can change.
claims.quote: it is a reading list the reader wears, and can change

claims.text: Anyone with a private persona link can open it, the same as a forwarded email; the persona holds reading suggestions, not secrets.
claims.quote: the persona holds reading suggestions, not secrets

claims.text: The page says where a persona came from and marks any vault that is not the newsroom's own, so a forged persona cannot pass itself off as ours.
claims.quote: so a forged persona cannot pass itself off as ours

claims.text: There is no analytics, by design; what the newsroom will know is what readers send through the share page and whether people write back.
claims.quote: There is no analytics, by design.

claims.text: To build: the vault with a published read key, the pages, follow and fork and remove in the next SG Meter, a keeper role with a behaviour policy, private personas, and outside reading.
claims.quote: A newsroom role with a behaviour policy: what it may change, how it records each change

claims.text: It should be built at newsroom.sgit.ai after the reader account has moved; the vault and the schema can be made first.
claims.quote: The vault and the schema can be made first, because they do not depend on which site reads them.

claims.text: It demonstrates what the site is about: content that changes without a deploy, shared with those who hold the key, decrypted in the browser, kept by agents whose every change is a commit.
claims.quote: Content that changes without a deploy, shared with exactly the people who hold the key

claims.text: The article was written from a voice note by Dinis Cruz by a Claude Code session working as the newsroom on 10 October 2026.
claims.quote: by a Claude Code session working as the sgit.ai newsroom, on 10 October 2026

claims.text: Apple's and Brave's descriptions of their own products are their claims, not independent audits.
claims.quote: are their claims, not independent audits

claims.text: A link to the front page lands a reader on a page made for nobody: sixty-odd pieces across six topics, with no way to know which they would want.
claims.quote: they land on a page made for nobody in particular

claims.text: Our agents already have dedicated resources with a small blast radius: their own mailbox, their own code-host account, their own Claude account.
claims.quote: Our agents already have dedicated resources with a small blast radius

claims.text: The next dedicated resource is a desktop of the agent's own, and it should be a Mac, because that is where most agent desktop apps arrive first.
claims.quote: The next one is a desktop of their own, and it should be a Mac

claims.text: This is a business plan for somebody else to build; it names no provider, and the whole plan with numbers, policies and a calculator is in the Agent Desk vault.
claims.quote: This is a business plan for somebody else to build

claims.text: The owner does not run agents on his own laptop because everything he has is on it.
claims.quote: because everything I have is on it

claims.text: Windows and Linux run as virtual machines by the hour from many places and a Mac never has; that gap is the business.
claims.quote: a Mac never has been. That gap is the business.

claims.text: Apple's licence allows leasing a Mac only for the sole purpose of providing Permitted Developer Services, such as continuous integration and building software.
claims.quote: for the sole purpose of providing Permitted Developer Services

claims.text: Each lease period must be at least twenty-four consecutive hours, to one customer with sole and exclusive use and control.
claims.quote: Each lease period must be for a minimum period of twenty-four (24) consecutive hours

value.unit: hours minimum per Mac lease

claims.text: Up to two additional virtual copies of macOS are allowed on a Mac you own or control, and not for time-sharing or service bureau use.
claims.quote: Up to two additional copies in virtual machines on a Mac you own or control

value.unit: additional virtual copies of macOS per Mac

claims.text: A shared pool of Macs whose desktops are rented by the minute to many customers for general agent work is not allowed.
claims.quote: So a shared pool of Macs whose desktops are rented by the minute to many customers, for general agent work, is out.

claims.text: The macOS 27 licence opens its virtualisation and leasing clauses with an exception for terms provided in writing by Apple, a route to written terms.
claims.quote: which is a route to written terms for a use Apple wants to support

claims.text: The plan recommends building a dedicated Mac run for the customer and developer agents, giving away the software, asking Apple for terms, and not building the pool.
claims.quote: build A and C, give away E, ask for D, and do not build the pool

claims.text: Per-minute pricing survives as a meter on a Mac one customer holds, never as a share of a Mac that others use.
claims.quote: Per-minute pricing survives, as a meter on a Mac one customer holds, never as a share of a Mac that others use.

claims.text: Each run boots a clean macOS, installs sgit, is given one key and clones one set-up vault; a small signed program in it does the rest.
claims.quote: Boot a clean macOS, install sgit, give it one key, and clone one set-up vault.

claims.text: The vaults divide the work like a supply chain, each party holding only its slice: set-up, code and data, a mandate vault, keys by PKI, and an audit vault.
claims.quote: The vaults divide the work, the way a supply chain should, with each party holding only its slice

claims.text: Each desktop has its own key pair and the vault keys it needs are encrypted to its public key, which is authorisation by encryption rather than by privilege.
claims.quote: Each desktop has its own key pair; the vault keys it needs are encrypted to its public key

claims.text: The bootstrap's key-handling steps were run with sgit 0.20.0 on Linux; nothing has run on a Mac yet.
claims.quote: Nothing has run on a Mac yet; the plan says so.

claims.text: For the same customer service agent, the excess over the mandate that nothing bounds is 23 rows of a 33-row grant on your own Mac, 11 on a dedicated Mac and 3 on a hardened one.
claims.quote: the excess nothing bounds falls from 23 rows to 11 to 3

value.unit: unbounded rows of the grant on your own Mac

claims.text: Of 22 hostile inputs, a boundary or an empty grant stops none on your own Mac, 2 on a dedicated Mac and 12 on a hardened one.
claims.quote: Hostile inputs stopped by a boundary or an empty grant, of 22

value.unit: hostile inputs stopped on the hardened Mac

claims.text: On your own Mac the behaviour policy is enormous because the grant is everything you have, and nothing is held by a boundary.
claims.quote: because the grant is everything you have: your mail, your files, your browser sessions, your keychain, your messages

claims.text: On a hardened Mac third-party controls do the rest: a supervised standard account, an egress proxy for the mandate's hosts, a binary allowlist, a mail gateway and every event streamed to the audit vault.
claims.quote: an egress proxy that allows only the mandate's hosts, a binary allowlist

claims.text: What is left on the hardened Mac is mostly the shop's admin screen, a finding about the shop's software, and screen recording, which a profile cannot grant.
claims.quote: That is a finding about the shop's software, not about the desktop

claims.text: For about 104 desktop hours a month, a dedicated Mac with the meter costs about £211 a month, a Mac mini run yourself about £119, and daily leases about £390.
claims.quote: a dedicated Mac with the meter costs about £211 a month

value.unit: GBP a month for a dedicated Mac with the meter

claims.text: The dedicated Mac wins once looking after your own takes more than about four hours a month, and beats daily leases once you need a Mac on more than about twelve days a month.
claims.quote: The dedicated Mac wins once looking after your own takes more than about four hours a month

claims.text: On the map, the agent's desktop moves from custom-built to product on parts that are already products or commodities: Apple silicon, the macOS virtual machine, the models, the desktop agent apps.
claims.quote: The agent's desktop moves from custom-built to product, on parts that are already products or commodities

claims.text: The plan asks a Mac host for dedicated Macs per customer with an erase API, a meter inside, a developer-agent offer, a joint approach to Apple for written terms, and an open stack.
claims.quote: A joint approach to Apple for written terms covering agent desktops

claims.text: Write the behaviour policy before the product: it is the argument, and it tells you which controls matter.
claims.quote: Write the behaviour policy before the product: it is the argument, and it tells you which controls matter.

claims.text: The plan assumes about five minutes from request to a working desktop, and the boot has not been timed yet.
claims.quote: it has not been timed yet

claims.text: Queueing many agents on one Mac satisfies one user at a time; the purpose of the lease and who the user is decide the rest.
claims.quote: Queueing satisfies "one user at a time"; the purpose of a lease, and who the user is, decide the rest.

claims.text: A queue of coding agents on a leased Mac fits the licence like a continuous integration runner; a queue of office agents is outside the lease however carefully scheduled.
claims.quote: A queue of office agents, working in mail, a browser and desktop apps, is outside the lease however carefully it is scheduled.

claims.text: If customers' own agents get slots on the operator's Mac, that is the time-sharing the licence excludes, and each customer would need a lease of at least 24 hours.
claims.quote: each of them would need a lease of their own of at least 24 hours

claims.text: The refinement: a dedicated Mac per customer is needed when the agents are the customer's; when the agents are the operator's, one Mac can serve many of them in turn.
claims.quote: When the agents are the operator's, doing work the customer buys, one Mac can serve many of them in turn

claims.text: The licence quotes are from Apple's macOS 15, 26 and 27 licences; the reading of them is ours and is not legal advice.
claims.quote: the reading of them is ours and is not legal advice

claims.text: Mac prices are from Apple's UK store on 9 October 2026; every other number is an assumption, labelled in the vault.
claims.quote: every other number is an assumption, labelled in the vault

claims.text: The article was drafted from a voice memo by Dinis Cruz by agent@riskmandate.ai, running Claude Opus 5.5, on 9 October 2026.
claims.quote: by agent@riskmandate.ai (Claude Opus 5.5, claude-opus-5-5) in the sgit.ai site session, on 9 October 2026

claims.text: Claude's desktop app and Cowork are very capable on a desktop, and Claude can drive desktop applications well: mail, messages, a browser, creative and video tools.
claims.quote: Claude's desktop app and Cowork are very capable on a desktop

claims.text: Every page on sgit.ai now has a price of a few pence, and a meter in the corner of the screen debits it from five pounds of starting credit.
claims.quote: Every page on sgit.ai now has a price, a few pence

claims.text: All of it lives in the reader's browser and nowhere else: no account, no server, no card, nothing sent.
claims.quote: no account, no server, no card, nothing sent

claims.text: A private window restarts the meter at five pounds, but also with no history, and the history is what the site uses to pick articles for the reader.
claims.quote: it also starts again with no history, and the history is what the site uses to pick articles for you

claims.text: Whether people would make the trade, pay a little, keep the record on their own machine and get a site that knows them back, is the question worth testing.
claims.quote: Whether people would make that trade is the question worth testing

claims.text: The meter has since gone live: it charges by how much of a page you read, the balance can go below zero with nothing blocked, a page can be declined with a reason, and topping up is a £5 Stripe payment.
claims.quote: it charges by how much of a page you read, your balance can go below zero with nothing blocked

claims.text: In the live version prices rose to 10p and 5p for articles.
claims.quote: Prices rose to 10p and 5p for articles.

value.unit: pence for a recent article in the live meter

claims.text: In the first version an article published in the last seven days costs 5p, an older one 3p, a newsletter issue, desk note or collection 2p, any other page 1p, and the homepage is free.
claims.quote: An article published in the last seven days costs 5p, an older one 3p

value.unit: pence for an article published in the last seven days

claims.text: The reader starts with £5.00 of credit, each page is debited once per visit, and going back to a page in the same session costs nothing.
claims.quote: and each page you open is debited once per visit

value.unit: GBP of starting credit

claims.text: Out of credit nothing is blocked: the page is shown, the read is recorded as unpaid, and a bar offers a top-up.
claims.quote: The page is shown, the read is recorded as unpaid, and a bar offers a top-up.

claims.text: Topping up has every step of a real shop except the payment: four packs, a cart, a review step, a confirm button and a receipt.
claims.quote: has every step of a real shop except the payment

claims.text: The list of what you read, with topics, is enough to personalise the site: the account and the front page pick unread articles from the topics read most, in a Picked for you band.
claims.quote: That list is enough to personalise the site.

claims.text: The browser does the arithmetic from the published articles/graphs.json, and the history never leaves the machine it was made on.
claims.quote: The history never leaves the machine it was made on.

claims.text: The meter can be escaped but the personalisation cannot be copied; the experiment is whether a site that knows what you read makes a few pence a page feel fair.
claims.quote: The meter can be escaped; the personalisation cannot be copied.

claims.text: A meter that charges nothing is the cheapest honest way to ask the question: price it, show the price, and give it away to people who know you.
claims.quote: Because it is the cheapest honest way to ask the question.

claims.text: The idea is old, 402 Payment Required was reserved in 1997; this meter asks whether the interesting part is the payment at all or what the reader gets back for the record of having paid.
claims.quote: whether the interesting part is the payment at all, or what the reader gets back for the record of having paid

claims.text: The first version was on the Portuguese newsroom: one cent a page, a five-euro wallet that refills itself, and a ledger page of its own.
claims.quote: one cent a page, a five-euro wallet that refills itself when it empties

claims.text: The Portuguese rules are kept: say it is a demonstration, never block a page, charge once per page per visit, and work if the browser refuses to store anything.
claims.quote: never block a page, charge once per page per visit so the back button is not a purchase

claims.text: Prices depend on what a page is and how new it is, set in one place in the site's build so the published table and the meter cannot disagree.
claims.quote: set in one place in the site's build so the published table and the meter cannot disagree

claims.text: The meter holds no money; anybody can edit their balance in developer tools, and real money would need a server or receipts signed by one.
claims.quote: Anybody can edit their own balance in the browser's developer tools.

claims.text: It does not follow the reader between devices; the history stays where it was made.
claims.quote: The history stays where it was made.

claims.text: A version that syncs could keep the ledger in an encrypted vault only the reader holds the key to; that is a proposal, not something built.
claims.quote: that is a proposal, not something built

claims.text: It does not meter agents: reading a page's markdown twin or the newsroom's wire costs nothing.
claims.quote: It does not meter agents.

claims.text: It charges the same for every reader; the obvious next prices are per question rather than per page.
claims.quote: The obvious next prices are not per page but per question

claims.text: The article was drafted from a voice note by Dinis Cruz by a Claude Code session working as the newsroom on 10 October 2026; the meter is assets/meter.js.
claims.quote: by a Claude Code session working as the sgit.ai newsroom, on 10 October 2026

claims.text: The browser is the biggest program most of us run, the largest attack surface on the machine, and the place we now want to put agents.
claims.quote: The browser is the biggest program most of us run, the largest attack surface on the machine

claims.text: A minimal viable browser has a small kernel, reviewed hardest and changed least, and loads components only when a page or an agent needs them, so its attack surface grows only as it is used.
claims.quote: A minimal viable browser has a small kernel, reviewed hardest and changed least

claims.text: Mozilla fixed 423 security bugs in Firefox in April 2026, against roughly 20 to 30 a month through 2025.
claims.quote: fixed 423 security bugs in Firefox in April 2026

value.unit: security bugs fixed in Firefox

claims.text: 271 of those bugs were found with an Anthropic model and fixed in Firefox 150: 180 rated high, 80 moderate, 11 low, a number of them sandbox escapes.
claims.quote: 271 of them were found with an Anthropic model and fixed in Firefox 150

value.unit: security bugs found with an Anthropic model

claims.text: Counted from NVD by filing organisation, Google's Chrome team filed 202 CVEs in 2025 and 3,246 in 2026 up to 17 October; Mozilla's filed 213 and 675.
claims.quote: Google's Chrome team filed 202 CVEs in 2025 and 3,246 in 2026 up to 17 October

value.unit: CVEs filed by Google's Chrome team in 2026

claims.text: Vendors already ship less code as a mode: Edge's enhanced security mode turns off the V8 just-in-time compiler, after Microsoft said 45% of V8 CVEs in 2019 were JIT-related.
claims.quote: 45% of V8 CVEs in 2019 were JIT-related

value.unit: percent of V8 CVEs that were JIT-related

claims.text: Edge's mode, Vanadium, Apple's Lockdown Mode and Tor Browser's Safest level are each a minimal browser for one threat, switched on by hand; the general version does not exist.
claims.quote: What does not exist is the general version: a browser that starts small and only grows when it has to.

claims.text: Three browsers come out of the same engine: one for an application with no extensions, media or downloads; one for an agent with no accounts or file access either; and the reader's own, loading what they use.
claims.quote: Three browsers come out of the same engine.

claims.text: Firefox has had pieces of this and dropped some: a site-specific browser removed in Firefox 86, a kiosk mode, site isolation since Firefox 95, and Servo now an embeddable library at 0.1.0.
claims.quote: Firefox has had pieces of this, and dropped some of them.

claims.text: The vendors say plainly that prompt injection will not be fixed: OpenAI says it is unlikely ever to be fully solved, Google calls indirect prompt injection the primary new threat, and Gartner says block AI browsers for now.
claims.quote: The vendors say plainly that this will not be fixed.

claims.text: In March 2026 Zenity Labs disclosed PleaseFix, a zero-click hijack of Perplexity's Comet through a calendar invite that reached local files; the fix was to restrict file access, a smaller browser.
claims.quote: The fix was to restrict file:// access: not a smarter model, a smaller browser.

claims.text: The better defences already point the same way: Atlas has a logged-out mode, Brave runs AI browsing in an isolated profile, and Chrome adds Agent Origin Sets that limit the sites a task can touch.
claims.quote: The better defences already point the same way.

claims.text: A browser for one agent is a practical prompt-injection defence: an agent cannot leak what its browser cannot reach, and the grant shrinks to the mandate.
claims.quote: An agent cannot leak what its browser cannot reach.

claims.text: LayerX's 2025 report found 99% of enterprise users have an extension installed and 53% have at least one with high or critical permissions.

claims.text: Sean Turner built a natural-language control policy for agent skills and a CI pipeline that checks every skill contributed to an organisation-wide repository against it before hundreds of developers pull it down.
claims.quote: a natural-language control policy for agent skills

claims.text: The control asks whether a contributed skill is safe, secure, well documented, usable, understandable by the model that loads it and by the people who review it.
claims.quote: is it safe, is it secure, is it well documented, is it usable

claims.text: What makes it more than a linter is that it reads the skill in its context: a LinkedIn skill working from internal documents has no prompt injection risk, a skill that pulls content off the internet reads untrusted text.
claims.quote: What makes it more than a linter is that it reads the skill in its context.

claims.text: The control is complementary to a security scan, not a replacement: a scanner asks whether a skill is malicious, the control asks whether this is the right way to give the skill to the workforce.
claims.quote: it is complementary to a security scan, not a replacement for one

claims.text: The owner describes the tool as Sean described it; he has not seen the code and could not find it published.
claims.quote: I have not seen the code, and I could not find it published.

claims.text: A skill is code nobody compiles: when an agent loads it, its instructions become part of what the agent does, with whatever the agent can reach.
claims.quote: a skill is code that nobody compiles

claims.text: Chainguard now publishes hardened agent skills with a record of the upstream commit, which makes a skill a trustworthy input but does not say what an agent running it should be allowed to do.
claims.quote: It does not say what an agent running it should be allowed to do.

claims.text: MongoDB's guide to reviewing a skill describes a structural validator in CI and an LLM judge on quality dimensions, none of which asks where a skill's inputs come from, and says no automated tool reasons across skill boundaries.
claims.quote: No automated tool currently reasons across skill boundaries.

claims.text: A skill described as an agent behaviour policy has a mandate, what it is for; a reach, everything it touches; a gap, which is the risk; and a barrier in front of each row of the gap.
claims.quote: Describe a skill that way and the context question answers itself.

claims.text: The LinkedIn skill's barrier is a person pressing publish; the web research skill's gap is following an instruction found inside a page, and its barrier has to be treating fetched text as data.
claims.quote: the barrier has to be treating fetched text as data

claims.text: A skill with untrusted inputs is one leg of Simon Willison's lethal trifecta; whether the agent loading it has the other two is a property of where it runs.
claims.quote: A skill with untrusted inputs is one leg.

claims.text: A control written in natural language and checked by a model is hope-based security: you give the model the rule and hope it follows it.
claims.quote: A control written in natural language, checked by a model, is what I call hope-based security.

claims.text: Hope or enforcement measured the cost for one customer service agent: built the obvious way, 97% of its rules were kept only by the model's good behaviour.
claims.quote: 97% of its rules were kept only by the model's good behaviour

value.unit: percent of one agent's rules kept only by the model

claims.text: A written control is still far better than none: it is the only place the intent exists, what a reviewer reads, what a model checks against, and what the deterministic rules are written from.
claims.quote: A written control is the only place the intent exists.

claims.text: Sean's next step: use an agent to write deterministic rules that follow the natural-language control; the model reads the control once and writes code that then runs the same way every time at no model cost per run.
claims.quote: Use an agent to write deterministic rules that follow the natural-language control.

claims.text: The description stays the canonical version, not the code: if the control changes, change the description and regenerate the code.
claims.quote: the description stays the canonical version, not the code

claims.text: The same round trip ran this week with Open Policy Agent, policy rows generated into Rego and parsed back, and AWS's agent policy service generates Cedar from plain English and checks it; intent stays the source.
claims.quote: people write intent, models write enforcement, and the intent stays the source

claims.text: Bring hundreds of skills to a common ontology, as fractal semantic graphs do, so that which skills read untrusted content, reach private data and can send it out becomes a query rather than a review.
claims.quote: Then the questions that matter across a catalogue are queries, not reviews.

claims.text: All of this is open source on our side and follows RiskMandate's line: a policy, a licence to operate that can be checked and revoked, and from a policy with a record, an insurable agent; we make agents insurable, we do not insure them.
claims.quote: we make agents insurable. We do not insure them.

claims.text: A skill with a policy, checked at contribution and enforced where it runs, is the smallest version of that whole chain, and Sean has built the first link.

claims.text: On 26 July 2017 the Supreme Court quashed the employment tribunal fees order in R (UNISON) v Lord Chancellor, holding it unlawful ab initio because the Act gave power to set fees but not fees that prevented access to justice.
claims.quote: the court held the order "unlawful ab initio", from the start, and said it "must be quashed".

claims.text: Every policy declares an envelope with the same fields at every altitude: money, blast radius, data in scope, people in scope, reversibility and duration, which is what makes the levels comparable.
claims.quote: The point is that the fields are the same at every level. That is what makes the levels comparable

claims.text: Where the envelope is numbers and lists, the check that a child fits inside its parent is mechanical, needs no model, and can run in CI on every change to a policy.
claims.quote: That check is deterministic, needs no model, and can run in CI on every change to a policy

claims.text: Where the envelope is words, a model can flag likely conflicts for a person to decide; it widens what a person can review and does not replace the review.
claims.quote: it widens what a person can review, it does not replace the review.

claims.text: The illustrative case is a VIP workflow refunding up to 1,000 GBP without a person, wider than the business limit of 100 GBP an order, so it is flagged as out of its powers before it runs.
claims.quote: The illustrative case in the figure is a "VIP" workflow that refunds up to 1,000 GBP without a person.

value.unit: GBP automatic refund limit proposed against the business limit

claims.text: A decision far outside the risk appetite shows up as an envelope that does not fit inside its parent's, whoever wrote it, which is how a business finds what nobody predicted.
claims.quote: A decision far outside its risk appetite shows up as an envelope that does not fit inside its parent's

claims.text: A kill switch sits at the altitude whose envelope it protects, escalation goes up one altitude, and a licence to operate is an envelope with a name.
claims.quote: A kill switch sits at the altitude whose envelope it protects.

claims.text: The 2,000 GBP daily circuit breaker belongs to the business level: it stops all automatic refunds, not one agent.
claims.quote: The 2,000 GBP daily circuit breaker belongs to the business level: it stops all automatic refunds, not one agent.

value.unit: GBP a day of automatic refunds

claims.text: Somebody still has to write the top: a risk appetite that says nothing measurable cannot be checked against, and the mechanical check is only as good as the numbers at the top.
claims.quote: The mechanical check is only as good as the numbers at the top.

claims.text: Envelopes can be gamed: a team can split one large refund into several small ones, so the envelope needs aggregate limits like the daily breaker, not only per-case ones.
claims.quote: A team can split one large refund into several small ones.

claims.text: Altitude is not hierarchy: the levels follow what is decided, not the org chart, and the person who owns a limit may not be the most senior.
claims.quote: The levels follow what is decided, not the org chart; the person who owns a limit may not be the most senior.

claims.text: Words stay hard: the model's flags are suggestions, and the decision is a person's.
claims.quote: The model's flags are suggestions; the decision is a person's.

claims.text: It is a proposal: no decision-policy format with envelopes exists yet, and the fields are the owner's.
claims.quote: No decision-policy format with envelopes exists yet; the fields above are mine.

claims.text: The numbers are illustrative: the tool's limits come from the third design in Hope or enforcement, and the levels above them are made up for the example.
claims.quote: the levels above them are made up for the example.

claims.text: The legal parallel is an analogy: courts and CI are different things, and the article borrows the shape, not the authority.
claims.quote: Courts and CI are different things; the article borrows the shape, not the authority.

claims.text: This is the second of four articles on agent decision policies, written from a voice memo of 17 October 2026 and checked by the site's agent, with editorial responsibility the owner's.
claims.quote: A voice memo from me on 17 October 2026, written up and checked by this site's agent; the editorial responsibility is mine.

claims.text: Most of the rules given to agents today are hope-based security: in the prompt or a policy it points to, holding only because the model follows them.
claims.quote: Most of the rules we give agents today are what I call hope-based security.

claims.text: Hope or enforcement measured one customer service agent built the obvious way: 97% of its rules were kept only by the model's good behaviour.
claims.quote: built the obvious way, 97% of its rules were kept only by the model's good behaviour.

value.unit: percent of rules kept only by the model

claims.text: In October 2026, are hooks the sweet spot between the prompt and real enforcement outside the agent, and how much of an agent's policy can move from the prompt into a hook now?
claims.quote: How much of an agent's policy can move from the prompt into a hook now?

claims.text: The agent writing this site works under a behaviour policy of eleven rules; ten say expectation, one is kept by a hook that supplies the status report, and one more is kept in part by a disabled push URL.
claims.quote: Ten of the eleven say expectation.

value.unit: rules kept by expectation

claims.text: The commit that published the first hooks article carried the wrong model name in its trailer: the leak scan looks for model ids, not names, and nothing compared the two, exactly the slip a hook exists to catch.
claims.quote: It is a small slip, and exactly the kind a hook exists to catch.

claims.text: In a throwaway repository with two bare remotes, one hook was written per rule and fed fixed JSON inputs a harness would send, without changing the session's own settings.
claims.quote: I wrote one small hook per rule and fed each one fixed inputs, the JSON a harness would send.

claims.text: Moved into hooks and tested: four rules fully, two mostly, three partly, two not at all.
claims.quote: Four fully, two mostly, three partly, two not at all.

value.unit: rules moved fully into hooks

claims.text: The leak-scan hook let a clean change through and blocked AWS's documented example key, but let a GitHub token shape through because the scan's patterns do not know that shape; a hook is only as good as the check it runs.
claims.quote: A hook is only as good as the check it runs.

claims.text: The output-masking hook cannot prevent anything: Claude Code's reference says the tool has already run by the time the hook fires.
claims.quote: The tool has already run by the time the hook fires.

claims.text: Hooks are the sweet spot for now: the first layer that does not depend on the model, and the last that still sees the action as the agent meant it, a tool call by name, a commit with its message.
claims.quote: They are the first layer that does not depend on the model: the same input gets the same answer every time, at no model cost.

claims.text: The vendors say the limits plainly: Trail of Bits says hooks are not a security boundary and a prompt injection can work around them, and on Claude Code a policy hook with a wrong path or a crashing script lets everything through by default.
claims.quote: Hooks are not a security boundary -- a prompt injection can work around them.

claims.text: A hook is a setting in the policy's terms, and what matters is who can change it: a hook in a file the agent can write is very close to an expectation, and this session's own hooks live in a folder the agent can write.
claims.quote: This session's own hooks live in a folder the agent can write.

claims.text: A hook the organisation installs where the agent cannot write, with only managed hooks allowed to run and failure set to block, is as strong as a hook gets; it still runs on the same machine with the user's permissions.
claims.quote: is as strong as a hook gets. It still runs on the same machine with the user's permissions, and it still sees only what is routed through it.

claims.text: The platforms agree on composition: on Claude Code all matching hooks run in parallel and deny beats defer beats ask beats allow; Cursor merges the same way; Codex runs matching hooks concurrently.
claims.quote: All matching hooks run in parallel

claims.text: A hook pack should be a set of independent checks, one small hook per rule with one job, where the most restrictive answer wins, not a pipeline where one hook depends on another's output.
claims.quote: A hook pack should be a set of independent checks, not a pipeline.

claims.text: The open collections that exist are mostly about dangerous commands: Trail of Bits blocks rm -rf and direct pushes to main, the safety net blocks destructive git and file commands, and Lasso Security's hooks scan tool output for prompt injection.
claims.quote: The open collections that exist are mostly about dangerous commands.

claims.text: Generating hooks from a team's own rules has started: claudecode-rule2hook converts natural language rules, Anthropic's hookify plugin writes rules from an instruction or recent conversation, and AWS's AgentCore Policy turns plain English into Cedar at a gateway.
claims.quote: Off the machine, AWS's AgentCore Policy does the same for a gateway: rules in plain English become Cedar

claims.text: OWASP's Agent Control Standard, in the GenAI Security Project, defines how agent platforms expose middleware hooks and how safety policies are enforced through them, with allow, deny, modify, ask and defer decisions and a policy engine such as OPA or Cedar behind them.
claims.quote: defines how agent platforms expose middleware hooks and how safety policies can be enforced through them

claims.text: The Agent Control Standard is early: its own repository says two of its nineteen hook methods are evaluated live.
claims.quote: Two of ACS's nineteen hook methods are evaluated live

value.unit: hook methods evaluated live

claims.text: The useful contribution to OWASP is not a new project on hooks but real policies and real hooks to test the existing standard with.
claims.quote: one exists, and the useful contribution is real policies and real hooks to test it with.

claims.text: The whole loop to build: from the written policy, one row per rule, generate one hook per row with fixed inputs that must be allowed and blocked as tests, install the pack where the agent cannot write, then read the pack back against the policy.
claims.quote: every rule with no hook is still hope, and every hook with no rule is a control nobody can explain.

claims.text: The description stays the source, as Sean Turner's control for skills does: change the rule, regenerate the hook, rerun the tests; and since a hook answers allow, deny or ask like a gateway, the same rows can later be compiled for the gateway.
claims.quote: change the rule, regenerate the hook, rerun the tests.

claims.text: The barrier column of the policy records where each rule is kept today, so moving a rule off the machine is one edit, and the gap it leaves is visible.
claims.quote: The barrier column of the policy records where each rule is kept today, so moving a rule is one edit, and the gap it leaves is visible.

claims.text: We already need this for our own agents, which is the best reason to build it; a session with a written policy and a release process can be among the heaviest users of hooks, and every gap found is one a customer does not.
claims.quote: We already need this for our own agents, which is the best reason to build it.

claims.text: The tests were fixtures, not a live harness: each hook ran on the JSON a harness would send, in a throwaway repository, and the composition rules are from the vendors' documentation.
claims.quote: The tests were fixtures, not a live harness.

claims.text: Hooks are not a boundary: they run on the same machine with the user's permissions and see only what is routed through them; they make rules harder to break, not impossible.
claims.quote: they make rules harder to break, not impossible.

claims.text: The counts are for one policy: four, two, three and two are this session's eleven rules, and another policy will divide differently.
claims.quote: Four, two, three and two are this session's eleven rules; another policy will divide differently.

claims.text: The pack is a proposal: the generator, the tests on every change and the gateway compilation are not built.
claims.quote: The generator, the tests on every change and the gateway compilation are not built.

claims.text: Collections and products move fast; they were read on 14 October 2026, and star counts and features change.
claims.quote: Read on 14 October 2026; star counts and features change.

claims.text: The article was written from a voice memo of 14 October 2026 by the site's agent, with the hooks written and tested against this session's own policy and the quotes re-checked on the vendors' pages.
claims.quote: The hooks were written and tested for this article in a throwaway repository, against this session's own behaviour policy, without changing the session's settings.

claims.text: Chainguard keeps a public ledger of software supply-chain attacks on its AI threat protection page: 28 incidents from 28 May 2024 to 8 October 2026, 23 of them from 2026.
claims.quote: The list has 28 incidents, from 28 May 2024 to 8 October 2026.

value.unit: incidents

claims.text: Of the 28 incidents in the ledger, 23 are from 2026.
claims.quote: 23 of the 28 are from 2026.

value.unit: incidents from 2026

claims.text: Chainguard's framing is that a sophisticated supply chain attack used to need time, resources and a skilled team, and AI has removed all three constraints.
claims.quote: AI has removed all three constraints.

claims.text: Counting the vectors, an incident can have two: an install-time hook ran the payload in 17, a maintainer account or token was taken over in 16, a typosquat in 5, a CI workflow in 3, tags repointed in 3, dependency confusion in 2.
claims.quote: an install-time hook ran the payload in 17, a maintainer account or token was taken over in 16

value.unit: incidents where an install-time hook ran the payload

claims.text: In the Trivy incident compromised credentials force-pushed 75 of 76 version tags, and five days later credentials stolen through that breach published two backdoored versions of LiteLLM, a package with 280 million monthly downloads.
claims.quote: A security scanner's breach became an AI gateway's breach, five days later.

claims.text: An Agent Behaviour Policy has four columns: the reach, measured from what the agent is connected to; the mandate, what it was asked to do; the gap between them; and the barrier on each row of the gap.
claims.quote: the reach, measured from what the agent is connected to; the mandate, what it was asked to do; the gap between them; and the barrier on each row of the gap

claims.text: Read with those four columns, every row of the ledger is the same shape: a credential, a tag or a build step could do far more than it was meant to, and the attacker used the difference, reach beyond mandate.
claims.quote: By my reading, the other rows have the same shape.

claims.text: In the tensorlake row, a maintainer's token could publish any version of any package the maintainer owned, while the mandate was to publish releases of one SDK from a reviewed build.
claims.quote: the maintainer's token could publish any version of any package the maintainer owned.

claims.text: As far as the public accounts show, nobody had written down that these credentials were for one thing, so nothing could notice when they were used for another.
claims.quote: nobody had written down that these credentials were for one thing, so nothing could notice when they were used for another.

claims.text: By our reading, a consumer-side control, rebuilt from source, a cooldown, no install scripts, an allowlisted registry, pinned actions, would likely have held in 26 of the 28 incidents.
claims.quote: By our reading, one of these would likely have held in 26 of the 28.

value.unit: incidents a consumer-side control would likely have held

claims.text: A publisher-side mandate, trusted publishing, a scope per package, two people to release, short-lived tokens, pull request text as data, appears in 16 of the 28, and both kinds in 14.
claims.quote: One of these appears in 16. Only the publisher can do it, and every item is a mandate

value.unit: incidents a publisher-side mandate would likely have held

claims.text: The consumer side needs nobody's cooperation and is what Chainguard sells; the publisher side makes the bad publish impossible rather than detected, and in two incidents it is the only kind that helps.
claims.quote: The publisher side makes the bad publish impossible rather than detected.

claims.text: The same move as Hope or enforcement: the share of one customer service agent's rules kept only by good behaviour fell from 97% to 23% when the rules moved into the platform.
claims.quote: the share of its rules kept only by good behaviour fell from 97% to 23% when the rules moved into the platform.

value.unit: percent of rules kept by hope after the move

claims.text: The first incident in the ledger, May 2024, was a hallucinated package name, huggingface-cli, which ChatGPT repeatedly suggested; registered as a proof of concept, it was downloaded more than 30,000 times in three months.
claims.quote: registered the name as a proof of concept, and it was downloaded more than 30,000 times in three months.

claims.text: Chainguard's own agent fleet, skillup, opened 4,746 standards-fix pull requests across its repositories over eight weeks.
claims.quote: Over the last 8 weeks, across our repositories, skillup opened 4,746 standards-fix pull requests.

value.unit: pull requests in eight weeks

claims.text: A confidence bot graded 3,044 of those pull requests; of 1,117, it judged 840, 75.2%, low-risk and merged them with no human in the loop.
claims.quote: it judged 840 (75.2%) as low-risk and merged them with no human in the loop.

claims.quote: The mandate is there too, in good sentences, but it lives in prompts, bot configuration and a blog post.

claims.text: The supply chain for an agent needs three records, trusted inputs, a written mandate, and provable outputs and memory, and only the first has a market yet.
claims.quote: the supply chain for an agent needs three records, and only the first has a market yet.

claims.text: Chainguard's hardened agent skills come from a public registry where each skill ships a HARDENING.md recording the exact commit it was hardened from and whether its instructions were changed.

claims.quote: RiskMandate is the work of writing these down, per agent and per deployment, for the people who will be asked about them.

claims.quote: an encrypted, versioned vault per unit of work, with a branch per agent, a reviewed merge, content-addressed history, and a server that holds only ciphertext.

claims.quote: sgit is open source: Apache-2.0, pure Python, two runtime dependencies, published on PyPI and as a container image

claims.quote: Moving it onto a minimal, rebuilt base is a one-line change in its Dockerfile

claims.quote: The vectors, the reach and mandate readings and the barrier for each row are my reading, and they would draw some rows differently.

claims.quote: no control was tested against these attacks here.

claims.quote: The four-column reading is a lens, not an audit.

claims.quote: The image change is planned, not made.

claims.quote: the night before Chainguard Assemble London, written by this site's agent in the voice of this site from Chainguard's public pages

claims.text: On 10 October Satya Nadella published Models as Insider Risks in the Super Intelligence Era, which reads like a summary of what this site has argued since The ultimate insider on 30 September.
claims.quote: written by the CEO of the company that ships Copilot.

claims.text: His argument: we cannot trace a frontier model's behaviour back to a code path as we traced software, so treat models as insiders, with identity, least privilege, logs and containment, and separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it.
claims.quote: separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it.

claims.text: He proposes seven principles: model diversity, observe everything, verifiability, independent controls, independent auditability, containment and incident disclosure.
claims.quote: His seven principles follow from that.

claims.text: His core move is the enforcer test in one sentence: a control bounds a grant only if it is enforced by something the grant does not include.
claims.quote: a control bounds a grant only if it is enforced by something the grant does not include.

claims.text: On 9 October two emails drafted by an agent went out in the owner's voice; the fix, built the same day, is a second reader the agent cannot skip, code checks first, then a fresh model call that fails closed.
claims.quote: On 9 October, two emails drafted by one of my agents went out in my voice.

claims.text: The second reader is a different model from the author: the drafter runs on Opus and the checker on Sonnet, so they do not share every blind spot.
claims.quote: the drafter runs on Opus and the checker on Sonnet, so they do not share every blind spot.

claims.text: Diversity of models is half of it; the other half is diversity of context, because a second model that has read the same poisoned email as the first is not independent however different its weights.
claims.quote: A second model that has read the same poisoned email as the first is not independent, however different its weights are.

claims.text: The agent team keeps its memory in encrypted vaults whose history is the record, append lanes let an agent write what it cannot read back, and re-anchoring adds a canary status report computed from the transcript.
claims.quote: the writer cannot edit what it wrote.

claims.text: Evidence should not be held by the party being observed, which is why the record sits in vaults whose host stores ciphertext and never holds a key.
claims.quote: Evidence should not be held by the party being observed

claims.text: Hope or enforcement runs the same 62 emails, sixteen hostile, through three designs of one agent: in the first design all 138 hostile tests rested on the model; in the third, 52 of 85 were held by a boundary.
claims.quote: in the first design, all 138 hostile tests rested on the model; in the third, 52 of 85 were held by a boundary.

claims.text: Synthetic users driving a real browser found bugs every test had passed over: two shipped JavaScript errors on riskmandate.ai, and on newsroom.sgit.ai a missing image that led to 51 of 527 figures across 10 articles not surviving the move.
claims.quote: checking it showed 51 of the 527 figures across 10 articles had not survived the move.

value.unit: figures that had not survived the move

claims.quote: Hope or enforcement is a deterministic simulation; no model was called. It tests the design, not a running agent.

claims.text: An Agent Behaviour Policy writes down four things for one agent in one deployment: the reach, measured; the mandate; the gap, derived and never written by hand; and the barriers, typed as boundary, setting, expectation or nothing, and only a boundary is a control.
claims.quote: Only a boundary is a control. The home page puts it in six words: a prompt asks, a policy enforces.

claims.text: In the published policy for Claude Code on the web with one repository attached, the agent can reach fifteen capabilities; six were asked for, and seven of the other nine have nothing real in the way.
claims.quote: the agent can reach fifteen capabilities; six of them were asked for, and seven of the other nine have nothing real in the way.

value.unit: unrequested capabilities with nothing real in the way

claims.quote: so it is a setting with a person's approval on record, not a boundary. Same code, different owner.

claims.text: The session that runs this site works under a ten-rule policy labelling each rule by what enforces it: nine are expectations, one is a setting, and none is a boundary.
claims.quote: nine are expectations, one is a setting, and none is a boundary.

claims.text: RiskMandate is deliberately not inline: it authors the policy and pre-commits what should happen, and the customer's own gateways, proxies, identity and scoped credentials enforce it.
claims.quote: An independent control should not be one more vendor in the request path.

claims.quote: Every vault on this site is published with its read key, on purpose

claims.text: The mandate should be locked under change control before the agent runs, so an auditor compares the footprint with a commitment, not a story, and the second reader's sources should come from somewhere the drafter cannot write.
claims.quote: so that an auditor compares the footprint with a commitment, not with a story.

claims.text: Every agent in the team is a session on a dedicated account, so the account is the blast radius; no agent sends, except the security agent, which may send one email to one address to put the whole team on hold.
claims.quote: the security agent may send one email, to one address, to put the whole team on hold.

claims.text: In the third design of Hope or enforcement, refunds stop at 100 GBP per order and a 2,000 GBP daily circuit breaker covers every automatic refund, so one bad day is bounded before it starts.
claims.quote: refunds stop at 100 GBP per order, and a 2,000 GBP daily circuit breaker covers every automatic refund

claims.text: A brake is only as good as the answers to who holds it, how long it takes, what it breaks and what it cannot reverse; containment without recoverability is a brake on a car with no reverse gear.
claims.quote: Containment without recoverability is a brake on a car with no reverse gear.

claims.quote: The agent went somewhere it was not asked to go, and nothing stopped it.

claims.text: Five things his list leaves out decide whether the principles work: the mandate, the deployment rather than the model, a named owner and an expiry, recoverability, and speed.
claims.quote: Read against our work, five things are missing, and each of them decides whether the seven work in practice.

claims.text: Observation tells you what an agent did and cannot tell you whether it was allowed to, unless somebody wrote down what it was for before it ran; compared with the footprint the mandate yields a near miss or a dormant mandate.
claims.quote: Observation tells you what an agent did. It cannot tell you whether the agent was allowed to

claims.text: Risk is a property of one agent in one deployment, not of the model: in Hope or enforcement the difference between a read-only tool bound to one customer and the broadest scopes is one customer against 38,000.
claims.quote: in Hope or enforcement, that difference is one customer against 38,000.

claims.quote: But a standard needs more than one small company behind it.

claims.text: The maturity table separates what runs today, what is published as design and what is only argued; the pattern is proven on a small real system and the products around it are early.
claims.quote: the pattern is proven on a small, real system; the products around it are early.

claims.text: Where to start: write the mandate before the agent runs, measure the reach, mark every rule with what enforces it and count the expectations, put a second reader on irreversible actions, journal every connector call, name the owner and expiry, and publish near misses.
claims.quote: Count the expectations. That count is how much of your policy is hope.

claims.text: His last line is that the most trustworthy system lets us trust the model least; the other half is that once you know how little you have to trust it, you can let it do a great deal more.
claims.quote: once you know exactly how little you have to trust it, you can let it do a great deal more.

claims.text: An agent in a separate Claude session read his post alongside this network's pages and drafted the answer, which this site's agent rewrote and added the week's events to; every claim about what runs links to the page that owns it.
claims.quote: Every claim about what runs links to the page that owns it; where something is design or only argued, it says so.

claims.quote: Hacking Portugal at 95%, last updated in December 2016; SecDevOps Risk Workflow at 64%; Generation Z Developers at 60%
