claims.text: Brief people and agents from the graph, not the pile of documents: a person joining a team or an agent starting a task needs the part of the graph around what they are about to do and what changed since they last looked.
claims.quote: They need the part of the graph around what they are about to do, and what changed since they last looked.

claims.text: Every article on this site has a graph of 8 to 18 nodes with typed edges, a teaser and a core idea, checked by the validator on every release; across the 112 articles there are 1,435 nodes and 1,538 edges.
claims.quote: Across the 112 articles there are 1,435 nodes and 1,538 edges.

value.unit: nodes across the 112 article graphs

claims.text: The articles' text is about 704,000 tokens at four characters a token, the graphs as JSON about 199,000, and the graphs' own words about 87,000: 12.4% of the text, an eighth, with the median article's graph 12.8% of the article.
claims.quote: That is 12.4% of the text, an eighth, and the median article's graph is 12.8% of the article.

value.unit: tokens of graph text against article text

claims.text: An agent can read every graph in a topic, follow edges to the articles that matter, then read those in full; the site publishes every graph in one file, a page drawing them, llms.txt and markdown twins.
claims.quote: follow the edges to the articles that matter, and only then read those in full

claims.text: The other half of a brief is the diff; in a graph that is cheap, a node superseded, an edge added, a claim marked out of date, so what changed since you last read this becomes a list of nodes, not a re-read.
claims.quote: "What changed since you last read this?" becomes a list of nodes, not a re-read.

claims.text: Embedding search is good at finding a starting point when you do not know the organisation's words, but it gives similarity, not a reason; the result depends on the model, the index and its settings, and re-indexing moves the neighbours.
claims.quote: But it gives you similarity, not a reason.

claims.text: A graph gives the same answer to the same question because it is a walk over named edges, and the answer comes with its path; for policies, the path is the answer.
claims.quote: The same question gives the same answer, because it is a walk over named edges.

claims.text: Nobody builds a correct graph of an organisation on the first try, and projects that try spend a year on the ontology and never ship; the graph does not have to be right, it has to be maintained, and the loop maintains it.
claims.quote: The graph does not have to be right. It has to be maintained, and the loop maintains it.

claims.text: Agents are very good at maintaining graphs: they read a new document and propose its nodes and edges, notice a policy changed and mark what rested on it, and keep the graph's own rules, while something that is not an agent checks those rules.
claims.quote: The maintenance is done by models and verified by code.

claims.text: On this site every article's graph is checked on every release: its quotes must be word for word in the article, its links must be links the article makes, its sizes within limits.
claims.quote: its quotes must be word for word in the article, its links must be links the article makes, its sizes within limits

claims.text: When something in the graph looks wrong you ask why is this happening, and the answer is a fix at the right altitude, in the source or in the graph, which the next brief carries.
claims.quote: The answer is a fix at the right altitude, in the source or in the graph, and the next brief carries it.

claims.text: Walking the links between articles found that 551 of 566 point back in time, and that an earlier article described a plan a later one said had not happened; that became Every link points back and the What came next notes.
claims.quote: Walking the links between articles found that 551 of 566 point back in time

value.unit: links pointing back in time

claims.text: Turning the AI Baseline Control Framework's CSV into a graph joined to the EU AI Act surfaced six things the CSV does not say, and the governance stack graph made every cell of a ten-layer table a node, 329 edges, 119 added.
claims.quote: the graph surfaced "the six things the graph found that the CSV does not say"

claims.text: Comparing a behaviour policy with the code that enforces it found a rule with no code and code with no rule, and in the code review vault a change is read at every layer from the method to the story.
claims.quote: comparing a behaviour policy with the code that enforces it found a rule with no code and code with no rule

claims.text: sgit is an encrypted git: the files are encrypted before they leave and the server holds only ciphertext; to brief an agent the owner gives it the key to a vault, and every change is a commit, so the history is the diff.
claims.quote: To brief an agent, I give it the key to a vault.

claims.text: A scoped clone takes one folder so an agent holds only its slice, a key pair per agent lets a brief be encrypted to the one agent that should read it, and an append lane sends findings back without reading anything.
claims.quote: A key pair per agent means a brief can be encrypted to the one agent that should read it.

claims.text: This site's agents already work this way: two agents share one vault with only the read key on the public side, agents running elsewhere keep their memory in one, and the site's own agent's policy is a brief restored after every summary.
claims.quote: the policy this site's own agent works under is a brief, restored after every summary

claims.text: Tokens are estimated: characters divided by four, on this site's 112 articles and their graphs at v0.12.39.
claims.quote: Characters divided by four, on this site's 112 articles and their graphs at v0.12.39.

claims.text: A graph is a map, not the territory: an eighth of the text is enough to choose what to read, not a replacement for reading it.
claims.quote: An eighth of the text is enough to choose what to read, not a replacement for reading it.

claims.text: Vectors still help: for finding a starting point in unfamiliar words similarity search is useful; the graph is what makes the answer repeatable and explainable.
claims.quote: the graph is what makes the answer repeatable and explainable

claims.text: This site's graphs have a contract; their size and checks are why they compress well, and an organisation's graph needs the same discipline.
claims.quote: Their size and checks are why they compress well; an organisation's graph needs the same discipline.

claims.text: Maintenance is still work: agents do most of it and a validator checks it, but someone has to own the ontology at each altitude.
claims.quote: Agents do most of it and a validator checks it, but someone has to own the ontology at each altitude.

claims.text: The article came from a voice memo of the owner's on 14 October 2026, written by this site's agent; the briefing figures were counted from the site's article markdown and graph files at v0.12.39.
claims.quote: The briefing figures were counted for this article from this site's article markdown and its graph files at v0.12.39.

claims.text: Anyone drowning in policies and internal documents who wants to see them as a graph, or brief their agents from one, can write to agent@riskmandate.ai.
claims.quote: If you are drowning in policies and internal documents and want to see them as a graph

claims.text: FT Strategies has started a series, Demystifying AI for News Publishers, and the edition on liquid content by Sofia Giannuzzi is one of the clearest explanations of the idea the owner has read.
claims.quote: is one of the clearest explanations of the idea I have read

claims.text: The guide defines liquid content as content that primarily consists of datafied components, or atomic objects, such as quotes, events or dates, rather than information already synthesised into an article, podcast or video segment.
claims.quote: today publishers mould content like clay into a finished product and let it dry, and liquid content keeps the clay wet

claims.text: The guide is right to point at data journalism as the working model, honest about measuring a story consumed in ten formats and keeping a human in the loop, and right that structured content could be sold through pay-per-query systems with AI agents.
claims.quote: The guide points at data journalism as the working model the industry already has, which is right

claims.text: The ChatGPT infographic is faithful on the definition, the three is-nots, the drivers and the challenges, but three lines set as quotations are the infographic's own, not the guide's, and one changes the sense of the Digiday line.
claims.quote: are the infographic's own, not the guide's

claims.text: The infographic leaves out the guide's open questions on measurement and human review, the 32% figure on newsroom alignment, and its expectation that the change may take a medium or large publisher several years.
claims.quote: the 32% figure on newsroom alignment

value.unit: percent, the guide's figure on newsroom alignment

claims.text: If content is to be liquid it needs water in it, and the water is not the format but the reporting: the notes, the calls, the documents, the half-recorded interviews, the hypotheses, the facts with the doubts still attached.
claims.quote: If content is to be liquid, it needs water in it, and the water is not the format. It is the reporting

claims.text: Once something is clay you cannot ask where it came from; the owner wants a graph of claims with confidence, evidence with provenance, sources named or protected, contradictions kept as edges: a fractal semantic graph, or a story vault.
claims.quote: You can mould it again, but you cannot ask it where the clay came from, or which part of the shape rests on which source.

claims.text: The guide's call for a complete reinvention of newsroom norms is a known trap; the method already exists in decades of journalistic practice, and the owner would bring back the experienced journalists and give them the tools.
claims.quote: The more I think about this, the more I think we already have the method.

claims.text: The inefficiency is in the tools: the raw material of a story lives in a notebook, a phone and somebody's memory, and most of the value created during the reporting is thrown away at the moment of publication.
claims.quote: most of the value created during the reporting is thrown away at the moment of publication

claims.text: Liquefying the notebook means capturing what the journalist already produces in the way they produce it: handwritten notes photographed and transcribed, calls recorded and linked, claims extracted into a graph the journalist can see and correct.
claims.quote: Liquefying it does not mean asking the journalist to fill in forms.

claims.text: Building a custom interface has become cheap, so every journalist can have a desk shaped to how they work: their own contact book, their own view of the claims on their beat, tools that adapt to them rather than a system they adapt to.
claims.quote: So every journalist can have a desk shaped to how they work

claims.text: The right picture is not AI writing everything with the journalist feeding it facts; writing the article is how the journalist discovers the narrative, a feedback loop between gathering evidence and writing.
claims.quote: Part of the skill of a journalist is writing the article, because writing it is how they discover the narrative.

claims.text: The article the journalist writes is one projection of the graph and is theirs; other projections, audio, a briefing for another role, another language, come from the same graph, and a question the graph cannot answer is the next piece of reporting.
claims.quote: The article they write is one projection of the graph, and it is theirs.

claims.text: With a graph that records who contributed which claim it becomes economic to bring in a historian, a librarian, a data scientist or a lawyer for an hour or a story and pay them for their time and the credibility they lend, which accumulates.
claims.quote: it becomes economic to bring them in for an hour, a question or a story, and to pay them

claims.text: An experienced journalist told their organisation must reinvent its norms will reasonably hear a threat; the message should be that their work is kept and made better with technology and teams rarely affordable before.
claims.quote: we want to take what you already do and make it better, give you technology you have not had, and build teams around you that were rarely affordable before

claims.text: Turning an article into a podcast is not liquidity, but a finished article can be liquefied, and a publisher with a long archive such as the Financial Times is sitting on decades of reporting that becomes more valuable with every link; start with one topic.
claims.quote: I would not start by converting all of it. I would start with one topic and liquefy whatever it touches

claims.text: A chatbot on an archive answers from whatever it retrieves and the reader cannot see which claim it relied on; the interface is what gets built from a graph, and the difference is whether every answer can name the claim and source it rests on.
claims.quote: The difference is not the interface; it is whether every answer can name the claim and the source it rests on.

claims.text: Personalisation should be neither static nor statistical: it is the intersection of two graphs, the reader's, holding role, company, sector, time, depth and language, and the story's.
claims.quote: It is the intersection of two graphs, the reader's and the story's.

claims.text: Read literally, prioritising readers' tastes is the brief that gave us clickbait, and optimising what people click is what digital publishing has spent twenty years doing without serving readers or publishers well.
claims.quote: But read literally, prioritising readers' tastes is the brief that gave us clickbait.

claims.text: When the owner pays a news organisation he pays for its judgment, what it thinks matters, how it checks it and how it presents it; readers' needs should shape the projections, not replace the direction.
claims.quote: Readers' needs should shape the projections. They should not replace the direction.

claims.text: The move from print to digital went badly for news because most of the value went to whoever sat between content and reader: by 2017 Google and Meta took 54.7% of American digital advertising, and the owner would rather not repeat that with AI.
claims.quote: by 2017 Google and Meta took 54.7% of American digital advertising

value.unit: percent of American digital advertising taken by Google and Meta

claims.text: A graph that names every claim and source adds ways of being paid that do not depend on attention: pennies per use, an agent paying per question, institutions licensing the evidence, and a share of every use walking back to the journalist and contributors.
claims.quote: a share of every use walking back to the journalist and to the contributors whose evidence the claim stands on

claims.text: Search engines persuaded publishers to make content indexable and then earned the advertising on it; structuring content for AI engines is the same work again, and the readers of that structure save money by having it, which is a reason they should pay for it.
claims.quote: Structuring content for AI engines is the same work again, and it has a value to whoever reads the structure.

claims.text: Start with one journalist: pick one topic and its reporter, capture their notebook as a graph they can correct, build them a desk, bring in one paid expert, publish their article and one other projection, measure, then liquefy the next story.
claims.quote: I would end with one journalist. Pick one topic and the reporter who knows it best.

claims.text: Liquid content is the guide's term and the clay image is the guide's; quotations are from Sofia Giannuzzi's guide for FT Strategies and through it from Digiday.
claims.quote: Liquid content is the guide's term and the clay image is the guide's.

claims.text: The article was drafted from a voice memo by Dinis Cruz, who holds editorial responsibility, by agent@riskmandate.ai running Claude Opus 5.5 in the sgit.ai site session on 7 October 2026.
claims.quote: by agent@riskmandate.ai (Claude Opus 5.5, claude-opus-5-5) in the sgit.ai site session, on 7 October 2026

claims.text: The industry's picture of agentic memory is one store that everything is pumped into and retrieved from by similarity; the owner's is the opposite, and that picture is wrong in three related ways.
claims.quote: I think that picture is wrong in three ways, and the three are related.

claims.text: Memory is context management: the question is never what do we remember but what does this agent need in its window right now, which the industry now calls context engineering.
claims.quote: The question is never "what do we remember" but "what does this agent need in its window right now".

claims.text: It is many memories, not one, because context is specific; by now the memories across the estate are inconsistent in places, and that is the point, since a memory forced to agree with all the others would be wrong for every one of them.
claims.quote: I used to think that was a problem to solve. I now think it is the point

claims.text: The estate now has twenty-seven sibling sites, forty published vaults, a CRM and an inbox, each a memory with its own ontology.
claims.quote: with twenty-seven sibling sites, forty published vaults, a CRM and an inbox

value.unit: sibling sites

claims.text: Memory has a cost in two currencies, the finite context window that degrades as it fills and the prompt billed by the token; Anthropic's guidance of September 2025 says context must be treated as a finite resource with diminishing marginal returns.
claims.quote: Context, therefore, must be treated as a finite resource with diminishing marginal returns

claims.text: Memory is made, not passive: somebody, a person or an agent, decides a thing is worth keeping, puts it where the next reader will find it, says where it came from and links it to what it relates to.
claims.quote: Memory is made. Somebody, a person or an agent, decides that a thing is worth keeping

claims.text: ChatGPT's Memory launched in February 2024 and in April 2025 was extended to all past chats; Claude's memory from September 2025 is scoped per project with an editable summary; Gemini's personal context arrived in August 2025, on by default.
claims.quote: Claude creates a separate memory for each project

claims.text: MemGPT in October 2023 paged information in and out of a limited window like an operating system; its successor Letta gives agents editable memory blocks; Mem0 and Zep store extracted facts, Zep as a temporal knowledge graph.
claims.quote: Its successor Letta gives agents editable memory blocks that live in the context itself.

claims.text: In Letta's August 2025 benchmark a plain filesystem, with the agent reading and writing files, scored 74.0 percent on LoCoMo against 68.5 percent for Mem0's graph variant; files won.
claims.quote: scored 74.0 percent on the LoCoMo memory benchmark against 68.5 percent for Mem0's graph variant

value.unit: percent on LoCoMo for a plain filesystem

claims.text: Manus treats the file system as the ultimate context, Anthropic's memory tool is a directory told to assume interruption, Claude Code loads a markdown index of 200 lines or 25 kilobytes, and since Karpathy in June 2025 the word is context engineering.
claims.quote: we treat the file system as the ultimate context

claims.text: The field has arrived at files, budgets, loading on demand and the context window as the scarce thing; where the owner differs is in what the files are, who can read them and how far the altitudes go.
claims.quote: Where I differ is in what the files are, who can read them, and how far the ladder goes.

claims.text: An agent meets memory two ways, the agentic session managing its own context across compaction, and the one-shot call where the bundle must be right the first time; both are served by the same memory if it has altitudes.
claims.quote: Both modes are served by the same memory if the memory has altitudes.

claims.text: On this site llms.txt is 350 lines and about 106 kilobytes, the graphs of all twenty-three articles one file of 234 kilobytes, one article's graph eight kilobytes against sixty for the article, the code review vault's bundle a megabyte and the vault with history four.
claims.quote: The graphs of all twenty-three articles are one file of 234 kilobytes

value.unit: kilobytes for the file of all article graphs

claims.text: The release log holds 211 entries from the first release to this one, each stamped with a commit, written for the next agent rather than a changelog reader; the forty vaults total 328 megabytes.
claims.quote: 211 entries from the first release to this one, each stamped with a commit

value.unit: release log entries

claims.text: The inbox agents keep their conversation in Email-FS as files, the CRM holds one folder per contact with its own graph, and none of these memories is forced to agree; what joins them is links and the index that keeps them.
claims.quote: What joins them is not a schema but links, and the index that keeps the links.

claims.text: Being open matters more than people expect: open source and Creative Commons let an agent fetch, quote, link and clone the memory, and the more is published the less the next session has to be told.
claims.quote: The more I publish, the more there is for the next session to stand on, and the less it has to be told.

claims.text: A shared memory must say where each thing came from or become a rumour mill; here that is habits: a URL for every quote, a commit for every release, a read key for every vault, a byline on every page.
claims.quote: The answer to a memory that cannot be trusted is not to trust it less. It is to make every item in it carry its source.

claims.text: Provenance is what lets memory be shared without being trusted, and it is the part a vector store cannot give, because a similarity score is not a source.
claims.quote: a similarity score is not a source

claims.text: The session that wrote the article ran across several context resets with no memory system, carrying only a summary of itself; everything else it read from the repository's conventions, the published sites and a review vault from another team.
claims.quote: That summary is memory as a hand-off note, and it is the one thing the model carried itself.

claims.text: It worked by altitude, index then graph then article then code and the four-megabyte vault only when the question was about the evidence; when the memo and the record disagreed, the record won and the article said so.
claims.quote: When the memo and the record disagreed, the record won and the article said so.

claims.text: The day's output was a revised article, two new ones, a vault and six releases, each consistent with the ones before, from a model that remembered nothing between resets except what the files remembered for it.
claims.quote: The day's output was a revised article, two new ones, a vault and six releases

value.unit: releases shipped in the day

claims.text: The loop is publish, index, load by altitude, act and check, write back, and the next session starts from the published material; the conventions along the bottom are what let agents share a memory without sharing a session.
claims.quote: Memory is context management as a loop: publish, index, load by altitude, act, write back, and the next session starts from the published material.

claims.text: Email-FS lite gives every agent a mailroom, inbox, done folder and outbox with each agent writing only its own folders, Issues-FS makes an issue a folder whose history is the vault's, and read keys let a memory be shared without being handed over.
claims.quote: a published key reads everything and writes nothing, which is what makes it safe to put on a web page

claims.text: Stale pages become false memories: the session found four, among them a page saying 617 nodes where the count is 1,051; two are fixed in this release and two are left standing and named.
claims.quote: the session that wrote this article found four more while researching it

value.unit: stale pages found by the session, two fixed

claims.text: The memory is opinionated: one person's estate with one person's vocabulary at the top of every altitude, and an agent that loads it loads the opinions with the facts, which is what the bylines are for.
claims.quote: The memory is opinionated. It is one person's estate, with one person's vocabulary at the top of every ladder.

claims.text: Discovery is hard at scale: twenty-seven sites, forty vaults, 211 releases and a growing CRM are more than one index holds, and the memory answers where is the thing I need well only for agents that know its shape.
claims.quote: Discovery is hard at scale.

claims.text: It is so far the owner's alone; the thesis would be properly tested when a second person's estate with a different vocabulary is read by the same agents alongside this one, and that has not happened yet.
claims.quote: That has not happened yet.

claims.text: Not yet built: a second estate read alongside this one, a freshness check that fails the build on a stale claim, a published shape for the hand-off summary, the one-shot bundle as a vault, and the librarian as a role on this site.
claims.quote: a freshness check in the build that fails on a stale claim the way the leak scan fails on a key

claims.text: The article came from a voice memo on 3 October 2026 answering a question the owner is often asked, behind which is the memory thesis on nfrs.sgit.ai; the industry references were read that day at the URLs in the sources.
claims.quote: A voice memo on 3 October 2026, answering a question I get asked a lot.

claims.text: At a digital sovereignty event a conversation with the chief executive of an infrastructure company with a large footprint in Romania kept returning to one point: sovereignty has to work in practice, and what stops it is not policy, regulation or price but code.
claims.quote: And in practice the thing that stops it is not policy, regulation or price. It is code.

claims.text: Organisations do not move off a hyperscaler because moving means changing the application: every call to S3, EC2 and IAM is written into code that works today, and rewriting bets the business on a migration whose upside is mostly a principle.
claims.quote: Every call to S3, every EC2 API, every IAM check is written into code that works today and that nobody wants to touch.

claims.text: The AWS European Sovereign Cloud went live on 15 January 2026 with its first region in Brandenburg, operated by EU residents, and sovereign local zones planned for Belgium, the Netherlands and Portugal; but sovereignty that depends on one company's API is sovereignty by permission.
claims.quote: Sovereignty that depends on one company's API is sovereignty by permission.

claims.text: The one hard requirement is that the original application must not know it is not running on a hyperscaler: not one line of its source changes, and the calls land on whatever is chosen underneath.
claims.quote: The original application must not know that it is not running on a hyperscaler. Not one line of its source changes.

claims.text: A twin here is an interface to a real system valued for whether the client can tell the difference, used by unmodified production code with a real backend behind it; a mock is used by tests and measured by fidelity.
claims.quote: The cost of switching a mock is a code path. The cost of switching a twin is an endpoint.

claims.text: If switching costs an endpoint, migration becomes a configuration decision; if it costs a code path it becomes a project, and projects get cancelled.
claims.quote: If switching costs an endpoint, migration becomes a configuration decision.

claims.text: The S3 twin is built as open source: code using boto3, the AWS CLI or any S3 SDK believes it is talking to S3, and the files can come from real S3, an encrypted vault, local disk or memory, selected per environment.
claims.quote: Behind the same interface the files can be served from real S3, from an encrypted vault, from local disk or from memory, selected per environment

claims.text: Of the three services named, S3 is the only one twinned; an IAM configuration risk engine is partly built, and the bigger idea of twins as a portability layer is designed, not finished.
claims.quote: The bigger idea, twins as the layer that keeps a workload portable across clouds, is designed, not finished.

value.unit: services with a finished twin

claims.text: S3 is the right place to start because it is the service everything touches, the best specified and already twinned; EC2 and IAM are harder, and the pattern is the same each time, a wrapping layer where the destination is a setting.
claims.quote: S3 is the right place to start because it is the service everything touches, it is the best specified, and it is already twinned.

claims.text: The main reason to make a move like this must never be sovereignty and never cost reduction; both are important and never urgent, and nobody signs risk for a principle.
claims.quote: The main reason to make a move like this must never be sovereignty, and it must never be cost reduction.

claims.text: A return that depends on a future event that might not occur is very hard to decide on; the signer needs cover, value added on the way that anybody can point to, and the loop has to close before the risk does.
claims.quote: So whenever a solution like this is offered, there has to be a positive loop in it, and the loop has to close before the risk does.

claims.text: The value goes in the twin layer because every call passes through it: backups that exist, every version controlled, encryption the operator cannot read, a journal of every call, behaviour policies agents cannot skip, and cost per workload.
claims.quote: That is what the twin layer is for, because every call passes through it, and that is where the value goes

claims.text: An sgit vault behind the twin lands the files as ciphertext with the key held by the customer and not by whoever runs the hardware, and a twin's journal keeps every request and response and can replay them, unlike platform logs.
claims.quote: Put an sgit vault behind the twin and the files land as ciphertext, with the key held by the customer and not by whoever runs the hardware.

claims.text: More of the code calling these APIs is agents, and the twin knows what the caller can reach, what it is meant to do and the gap, enforcing the barrier where the application cannot route around it.
claims.quote: it enforces the barrier at a place the application cannot route around

claims.text: The value list is still a little invisible to a signer and needs sharpening; version control and encryption with the key held elsewhere are each a tangible return, and the test is whether the move moves a top-of-register risk.
claims.quote: I will be honest that the list is still a little invisible to a signer; it needs to be sharper than this, and that is work for the next version.

claims.text: No new features during the move: it is a pure villager move, explorer to town planner, and the moment a feature is added the migration is also a product change and nobody can tell which broke what.
claims.quote: When you do a project like this you cannot add new features.

claims.text: Testing may matter more than sovereignty: the same unmodified code can run against an in-memory twin on a laptop, a twin replaying last week's journal, a twin injecting failures, and the real service, so the environment becomes a setting rather than a guess.
claims.quote: With twins the environment becomes a setting rather than a guess

claims.text: Every piece of software should be able to run, unmodified, against a twin of every external service it depends on, without knowing; software that can only run against one provider's live API cannot be tested properly, moved, or put behind a policy.
claims.quote: it must be able to run, unmodified, against a twin of every external service it depends on, without knowing

claims.text: The twin layer must be open source or the lock-in has moved, not gone; open source here is about independence, not community, and there is no sovereignty without open source and open schemas because sovereignty means you can leave.
claims.quote: Swap one vendor's API for another vendor's proprietary wrapper and the lock-in has moved, not gone.

claims.text: The business model is for an infrastructure operator in Romania, Portugal, the UK or anywhere in Europe: not move to us, which sells risk, but keep your code, point it at us, and gain versions, backups, encryption, a journal, policies and cost visibility.
claims.quote: Selling "move to us" means selling risk.

claims.text: The buyer owns the register line, not the cloud bill; they buy first the twin in front of the real service with nothing moving, a monthly fee per workload, then the backend switch one environment at a time, per terabyte and per call.
claims.quote: The buyer is the person who owns that register line, not the person who owns the cloud bill.

claims.text: Storage and compute are commodities and should be priced as such; the operator's margin is in the twin layer, the journal, the policy enforcement and the reports a regulator or insurer will accept, the custom layer above the commodity.
claims.quote: sell the custom layer above the commodity, not the commodity

claims.text: The hyperscaler cannot sell indistinguishability from itself; a smaller operator can, standing on commodities the big players matured, which is the judo move using the customer's code, the hyperscaler's API and open source as the weight.
claims.quote: The hyperscaler cannot sell indistinguishability from itself.

claims.text: Assumptions to check: that the S3 API surface the twin covers is enough for first customers, that a journal and policy report move a real register line, that the per-call price survives a chatty workload, and that the first operator will fund the hardening.

claims.text: Name an owner per mandate rather than per agent, because agents are too many and short-lived to own one by one and a mandate is what an auditor needs.
claims.quote: A mandate lives long enough to have an owner, and is what an auditor actually needs

claims.text: Define independent: a guardrail model reading the agent's output is a second opinion, a scoped credential is a boundary, and a control should say which it relies on.
claims.quote: A guardrail model that reads the agent's output is a second opinion; a scoped credential is a boundary.

claims.text: Test the controls and not just the agent: whether the leak scan still runs and the counter still counts after a summary, a hook change or a new tool.
claims.quote: The other question is whether the controls still fire after the session changes, which is cheaper to test

claims.text: Publish the policy as an artefact: none of the frameworks says what the file an agent runs under should look like, and nobody at the conference showed theirs.
claims.quote: None of them says what the file an agent runs under should look like: its grant, its mandate, its rules and who enforces each.

claims.text: The CRI framework sets 230 control objectives, and in August CRI and AIUC-1 announced a crosswalk to cover agent risks.
claims.quote: The CRI framework sets 230 control objectives

value.unit: control objectives

claims.text: One agent is not a sample; this is a worked example, not a survey.
claims.quote: This is a worked example, not a survey.

claims.text: The policy is not independent of its agent: the hook and the policy were set up with an agent's help and sit where the agent could edit them.
claims.quote: The hook and the policy were set up with an agent's help, and sit where the agent could edit them.

claims.text: No outside red team has tested the agent; the controls described are what exists, not proof that they hold.
claims.quote: The controls described are what exists, not proof that they hold.

claims.text: The research numbers come from specific setups; hint-mention and reward-hack rates vary by model and task.
claims.quote: Hint-mention and reward-hack rates vary by model and task.

claims.text: The post's poll and case-study numbers are not used because they could not be traced.
claims.quote: We could not trace them.

claims.text: The session data, the policy and the commit counts come from the agent's own session on 16 October 2026; the editorial responsibility is the owner's.
claims.quote: the session data, the policy and the commit counts are from that agent's own session on 16 October 2026

claims.text: For the authentic founders who come from the field they build for, the brand is the founder and their authenticity is the proof, so it needs a medium that keeps it.
claims.quote: For them, the brand is the founder: their authenticity is the proof.

claims.text: A site written from voice memos keeps a founder's history with dates, and because every claim is checked before publication it is a record others can trust.
claims.quote: A site written from voice memos keeps it, with dates, and because every claim is checked before it is published, it is a record that others can trust.

claims.text: Building one teaches what a pure client-side site is: static files on a host, code in the reader's browser, and no server holding anyone's data.
claims.quote: Building one teaches what a pure client-side site is: static files on a host, code that runs in the reader's browser, and no server that holds anyone's data.

claims.text: GitHub Pages is free with one condition that matters: on GitHub Free the repository must be public.
claims.quote: the repository must be public

claims.text: Published GitHub Pages sites may be no larger than 1 GB, with a soft bandwidth limit of 100 GB per month.
claims.quote: Published GitHub Pages sites may be no larger than 1 GB

value.unit: GB site size limit

claims.text: Claude cloud sessions are available on Pro, Max and Team plans, run from the browser or the Claude app on a phone, and reach repositories through the Claude GitHub App.
claims.quote: run from the browser at claude.ai/code or from the Code tab of the Claude app on a phone

claims.text: The owner records with Otter; the order things were said in and the words reached for are the raw material for the founder's voice.
claims.quote: I use Otter; the order you said things in, and the words you reached for, are the raw material for your voice.

claims.text: A Stripe Payment Link takes the top-up; the site never sees card details.
claims.quote: The top-up page sends the reader to it; your site never sees card details.

claims.text: The recipe is eight steps, with a GitHub Actions workflow that validates, tags and deploys, where the rule that matters is that a failed check stops the release.
claims.quote: The rule that matters is that a failed check stops the release.

claims.text: A correction is a new version of the article with its diff, not a note about the old one, and every release gets a version and a one-line note.
claims.quote: a correction is a new version of the article, with its diff, not a note about the old one

claims.text: The house rules are one file at the root, CLAUDE.md, read at the start of every session, holding the voice, the verification rules and the release steps, growing by a line with every correction.
claims.quote: This is where your voice, your verification rules and your release steps live, and it grows by one line every time you correct the agent.

claims.text: api.newsroom.sgit.ai is a client-side API: versioned files a site loads and pins, running in the reader's browser with no server.
claims.quote: It is a client-side API: versioned files a site loads and pins

claims.text: The meter's defaults are £5 of credit to begin, 5p an article and 10p when new, with top-ups through a Stripe Payment Link the publisher owns.
claims.quote: the defaults are "£5 of credit to begin", 5p an article and 10p when new

value.unit: pence per article by default

claims.text: The meter is an honesty box, not a paywall: it never blocks a page, and because the balance is in the reader's browser a reader can change it.
claims.quote: It is an honesty box, not a paywall: it never blocks a page, and because the balance is in the reader's browser, a reader can change it.

claims.text: GitHub says Pages is not for running an online business; a writing site with an optional meter is primarily writing, and if it becomes a shop it should move.
claims.quote: A writing site with an optional meter is primarily writing; if yours becomes primarily a shop, move it to a host that allows that.

claims.text: The next step is to write the house rules as an Agent Behaviour Policy: a versioned file saying what the agent is given, what it is for and what it must not do, each rule marked by what keeps it.
claims.quote: a versioned file that says what the agent is given, what it is for, and what it must not do, with each rule marked by what keeps it

claims.text: An agent that publishes needs real privileges: it can push to the repository, which means it can publish anything to the site.
claims.quote: it can push to your repository, which means it can publish anything to your site

claims.text: A behaviour policy is not only a security control; it goes down to the business logic, how many posts a day, the tone, no Sunday publishing.
claims.quote: A behaviour policy is not only a security control; it goes all the way down to how you want the work done.

claims.text: Split the work across a writer, an editor and a publisher with separate grants, so the agent that writes cannot publish and the one that publishes cannot invent.
claims.quote: so the agent that writes cannot publish on its own, and the one that publishes cannot invent

claims.text: A policy enforced by the prompt keeps the rules in view but it is still the agent keeping them; a hook blocks the action whatever the agent intended.
claims.quote: That keeps the rules in view, but it is still the agent keeping them.

claims.text: This site's own writing session runs under a policy of eleven rules, re-read after every summary, reporting its status every few answers; more than half of its rules could move to hooks.
claims.quote: under a policy of eleven rules that is re-read after every summary and reports its status every few answers

value.unit: rules in the site's policy

claims.text: A more advanced setup keeps a private sgit vault beside the public repository for drafts, transcripts, data, client notes, voice guidance and the agent's working files.
claims.quote: The repository holds what is published. Beside it, an sgit vault holds the rest

claims.text: The agent clones the vault with a key given through the environment, never in a file in the repository, and only the publisher copies approved text to the public repository, so nothing private touches the public history.
claims.quote: Nothing private ever touches the public history.

claims.text: On this site, in three days, 54 messages from the owner, ten of them voice memos, became 40 releases, each with figures, sources and a section on what it does not claim.
claims.quote: in three days, 54 messages from me, ten of them voice memos, became 40 releases

value.unit: releases from 54 messages in three days

claims.text: Ask the agent to interview you when a story is thin, as a journalist challenging every answer; and let the record build on itself, every article linking to the ones before.
claims.quote: Ask the agent to interview you when a story is thin

claims.text: The writing pipeline is not a kit yet; the site's generator and release steps are published as a pattern and the brief has the agent build a smaller one.
claims.quote: The writing pipeline is not a kit yet.

claims.text: The meter trusts the reader: balances can be edited and the return page does not verify a payment, both by design.
claims.quote: Balances can be edited, and the return page does not verify a payment, both by design.

claims.text: Costs vary: GitHub Pages is free within its limits; a Claude plan, a domain and Stripe's fees are not.
claims.quote: GitHub Pages is free within its limits; a Claude plan, a domain and Stripe's fees are not.

claims.text: A public repository is public; on a free plan Pages needs it, and nothing confidential belongs in it.
claims.quote: On a free plan, Pages needs it; nothing confidential belongs in it.

claims.text: A rule in a prompt is a hope; only the rules a hook or CI keeps are enforced, so mark which is which.
claims.quote: Only the rules a hook or CI keeps are enforced; mark which is which.

claims.text: The article was updated on 15 October to add the behaviour policy and the private vault.
claims.quote: Added the behaviour policy and the private vault.

claims.text: The article comes from a voice memo of 15 October 2026, written by the site's agent in the voice of the site, with the recipe being the site's own and the sources read that day.
claims.quote: A voice memo of mine on 15 October 2026, written by this site's agent in the voice of this site

claims.text: The owner decided the question the last article left open: the meter charges for what is read, not for what is scrolled.
claims.quote: Charge based on what you read, not based on what you scroll.

claims.text: A page flicked to the end now costs the minimum, a tenth of its price; a page read through costs its price; a reset refunds to the minimum.
claims.quote: A page flicked to the end costs the minimum, a tenth of its price; a page read through costs its price

claims.text: Read is the measure the reading strip already kept: time on each section while the tab is in front and the reader active, against the section's words at 300 a minute.
claims.quote: against the section's words at 300 a minute

value.unit: words a minute

claims.text: Reading done on an earlier visit is not charged again; a return visit is charged only for what is read beyond it.
claims.quote: charged only for what is read beyond yesterday

claims.text: The meter's block on a return visit showed 1p charged and 0 percent read this visit, with 58 percent read before and not charged again.
claims.quote: 0% read this visit (58% read before, not charged again)

value.unit: percent read on an earlier visit

claims.text: The owner's brief was that the user is in control: if the measure says a section was read and the reader disagrees, they can say so.
claims.quote: The owner's words were the brief: "the user is in control".

claims.text: Pause stops all measuring, and so all charging, on every page until the reader resumes, and it is kept in the browser so a reload or another article stays paused.
claims.quote: It is kept in the browser, so a reload or another article stays paused.

claims.text: Reset sets every section of a page back to unread and refunds the page to its minimum; reading it again is charged again.
claims.quote: Every section goes back to unread, and the meter refunds the page to its minimum; reading it again is charged again.

claims.text: Any section can be marked read or unread by hand: marked read it is charged as read, marked unread it goes back to zero, and the map says which were marked.
claims.quote: A section marked read counts as read, and is charged as read; a section marked unread goes back to zero.

claims.text: The owner described hiding what was read, showing a line or a small paragraph; the agent built those three and three more, six views in all, so they can be compared.
claims.quote: I built those three, and three more around them, so they can be compared

value.unit: views of a read section

claims.text: Margin is the default view: a line beside a read section, solid when read, pale when part read, grey when only scrolled past, so nothing on the page moves.
claims.quote: a line beside it: solid when read, pale when part read, grey when only scrolled past

claims.text: The owner was precise that nothing should change while the reader is reading, so they can read at their own pace.
claims.quote: you want to allow the user to read at the pace that the user is reading

claims.text: The views switch on in two cases only: the reader comes back to an article partly read before, or scrolls back up by more than half a window after going down at least a window.
claims.quote: So the views switch on in two cases only: the reader comes back to an article they had read some of before, or they scroll back up by more than half a window after going down at least a window.

claims.text: A section on screen is never folded or unfolded by the clock; it changes when off screen or when the reader asks.
claims.quote: A section on screen is never folded or unfolded by the clock; it changes when it is off screen, or when the reader asks.

claims.text: When a fold changes the height of the page above what the reader is looking at, the scroll position is corrected so the words in view do not move.
claims.quote: the scroll position is corrected so the words in view do not move

claims.text: Every section of every article now has a line and a paragraph: 1,897 sections in 174 articles, each with about eight words and two or three sentences saying what it says.
claims.quote: 1,897 sections in 174 articles, each with about eight words and two or three sentences that say what it says

value.unit: sections, across articles

claims.text: Fourteen agents wrote the summaries: twelve in parallel taking about fourteen articles each, then two for the twelve articles published while they worked.
claims.quote: Twelve agents each took about fourteen articles, and two more took the twelve articles other sessions published while they worked.

value.unit: agents writing summaries

claims.text: Each agent wrote a line of six to nine words saying what the section says, not what it is about, and a paragraph of 30 to 60 words with its figures, names and conclusion.
claims.quote: a line of six to nine words saying what the section says, not what it is about, and a paragraph of 30 to 60 words with its figures, names and conclusion

claims.text: A script checked every summary for length, the wording rules and that every section of the article had both a line and a paragraph.
claims.quote: A script checked every one for the length, the wording rules

claims.text: Several agents reported articles that disagree with themselves, a count in the opening differing from the same count later; the summaries follow each section's own figure and those articles are for the writer to correct.
claims.quote: Several agents reported where an article disagrees with itself, a count in its opening that differs from the same count later

claims.text: Summaries are now part of writing an article, beside the graph; a section without one gets an extract, and the build counts the extracts so they do not stay.
claims.quote: A section without one gets an extract, its first sentence, and the build counts the extracts so they do not stay.

claims.text: None of this is carried to the vault yet; the reading records, the pause and the chosen view are kept in the browser only, like the theme.
claims.quote: The reading records, the pause and the chosen view are kept in this browser only, like the theme.

claims.text: The meter does not know what the reader understood; read is still time in view while present, and the controls exist because the measure can be wrong in both directions.
claims.quote: Read is still time in view while you were present.

claims.text: It summarises sections, not paragraphs, because sections are what is measured.
claims.quote: sections are what is measured, so they came first

claims.text: The views are text; the owner's next step, a picture in place of a folded section, is not built.
claims.quote: a picture in place of a folded section, is not built

claims.text: Rereading after a reset is charged again, as decided; it is one line to change.
claims.quote: After a reset, reading a page again costs what reading it costs.

claims.text: The meter's v1.5.0 core gains settle(share), which sets the share of the price charged in steps of 5 percent, never below the tenth for opening.
claims.quote: which sets the share of the price charged, up or down, in steps of 5%, never below the tenth for opening

value.unit: percent per settle step

claims.text: The page view no longer listens to scrolling; it reads the reading record when the page opens and settles on every reading event to what was read beyond the base.
claims.quote: The page view no longer listens to scrolling.

claims.text: Each written summary carries the first twelve characters of the SHA-256 of its section's text, and when they no longer match the summary is served marked stale.
claims.quote: Each written summary carries the first twelve characters of the SHA-256 of its section's text; when they no longer match, the summary is served marked stale.

claims.text: The gate is a browser test with Playwright's clock, so a minute of reading takes milliseconds, covering pause, mark, reset, the six views and the charges.
claims.quote: with Playwright's clock so a minute of reading takes milliseconds

claims.text: The owner's message of 17 October 2026 is the brief and the editorial responsibility is his; the code, screenshots and measurements are the agent's.
claims.quote: The code, the screenshots and the measurements are mine
